hero.headline: Stuart downtown dock closes Sunday for $3 million renovation through July 2027
hero.teaser: Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for a year-long $3 million renovation that will nearly double capacity from 18 to 44 boat slips.
hero.body:
Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for a $3 million renovation projected to be complete by July 4, 2027. The project will nearly double the dock's capacity, expanding from 18 to 44 slips for motorized and non-motorized vessels. The renovation includes a 7,500 square foot fixed dock, a 1,400 square foot floating dock and a smaller floating platform. The project is funded by a state grant and transportation impact fees.

Stuart Mayor Sean Reed said the upgrades are designed to prevent storm damage during hurricanes and major storms. More than 1,400 boaters use the dock annually. During the closure, the city is working to accommodate businesses relying on the dock. Tiki Taxi & Cruises, which operates from the dock, will be allowed to build a gate at the end of the non-floating section to continue boarding passengers, according to Austin Kuyrkendall, the company's director of operations. Boat captain Parker Fisher said the dock has needed work for years and hopes to see more floating docks added to the facility.

cards.headline: DeSantis signs $117.6 billion Florida budget with $810 million in vetoes
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a $117.6 billion state budget this week, marking the fourth consecutive year of declining spending in Florida. The Governor vetoed nearly $810 million in line-item projects, exercising restraint compared to his record-breaking $3.1 billion in vetoes in 2022. DeSantis said he cut items considered either inappropriate or nice to have, focusing the budget on what he characterized as core state priorities.

The approved budget invests billions in road construction acceleration, teacher pay increases, and major cancer research initiatives. The spending plan sets aside $665 million for Everglades restoration efforts. However, DeSantis also blocked the Legislature's proposed $750 million transfer into the state's rainy-day fund, which lawmakers included to prepare for new requirements under a proposed constitutional amendment passed by the House last year that would increase the mandated cap on the budget stabilization fund.

Among the notable cuts, DeSantis vetoed $91.5 million intended to increase correctional officers' salaries. Government watchdog Florida TaxWatch had urged the Governor to eliminate 621 projects worth $830 million that the group labeled budget turkeys. DeSantis ultimately vetoed 184 of the 621 appropriations flagged by the organization.

The term-limited Governor indicated he will not formally lead any political committee to campaign for budget-related constitutional amendments after the Legislature modified his original proposals. DeSantis said that while he might participate if asked, he does not plan to spearhead efforts or take a leadership role in advocating for the changes. The new fiscal year budget took effect as DeSantis approaches the end of his final term as Florida's chief executive.

cards.headline: Record Fourth of July travel brings heavy traffic and rain to South Florida roads
cards.body:
A record-breaking number of Americans are hitting the roads this Fourth of July weekend, and South Florida drivers are contending with both massive crowds and heavy rain. AAA estimates that 72.2 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home between Saturday, June 27 and Sunday, July 5, marking an all-time high for the holiday. Of those travelers, 61.4 million are making the journey by car. Orlando and Miami rank among the top five travel destinations for Independence Day this year, according to AAA data. Friday's wet weather created challenging conditions on the Florida Turnpike south of Orlando as drivers began their holiday trips.

The combination of rain and congestion tested drivers' abilities on the roadways. Driver Ed Budd described the conditions as beautiful until the rain arrived, at which point he observed that everyone seemed to forget how to drive. Despite the challenging weather, most drivers pressed forward with their plans. Driver Jim Macfawn, who said he has considerable driving experience, explained that he simply rolls with the punches when dealing with difficult road conditions. Macfawn also reflected on the scale of holiday travel, expressing surprise at the number of people traveling given current gas prices.

Some drivers experienced very different outcomes on Friday's roads. Carlos Borras and his wife completed a round trip between Orlando and Miami without incident, reporting smooth sailing with no traffic or accidents encountered. Driver Fernando Amado painted a different picture, describing busy conditions that were made worse by the weather. Amado noted that Friday appeared to be the peak day for people heading north, contrary to what some might have expected.

For those still planning to travel, AAA offers guidance on timing. The organization recommends leaving after 3 p.m. on Saturday or before 11 a.m. on Sunday to avoid the worst congestion. Saturday's heaviest traffic is expected between 10 a.m., while Sunday will see peak congestion between noon and 6 p.m. According to AAA, your starting point, destination, and departure time all play significant roles in determining your travel experience. With record numbers of vehicles on South Florida roads this weekend, careful planning about when to travel can make a substantial difference in avoiding delays.

cards.headline: Juno Beach residents demand fence at JB-7 beach access as dispute heads to budget talks
cards.teaser: Colony Condos residents say beachgoers have been trespassing on private property since the town removed a fence at the JB-7 public beach access in 2023.
cards.body:
Residents at the Colony Condos in Juno Beach are demanding the town reinstall a fence at the JB-7 public beach access point after it was removed in 2023 for safety reasons. Without the barrier, only bushes now separate the public walkway from private property, and residents say summer beachgoers are cutting through their land with coolers, fishing rods and lawn chairs while parking in private spots. Lori Hill, a Colony resident, said confrontations with trespassers have become common, forcing residents to call police rather than confront visitors directly.

The dispute reached the Juno Beach Town Council at a recent meeting, where officials acknowledged the town is not obligated to install a fence. Vice Mayor Pro Tem DD Halpern suggested exploring lower-cost alternatives, including a combination of split rail fencing and shrubs. Hill expressed hope the town would reinstall the original fence to restore landscaping and private parking. The council agreed to address the fence question during budget discussions scheduled for July 15. Not all beachgoers agree the problem is significant, with some citing available free parking and questioning whether property damage is actually occurring.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk comments
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court challenge Thursday against an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate a teacher suspended last year .
cards.body:
The Martin County School Board is challenging an administrative law judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009 who was suspended last year over social media comments about conservative activist Charlie Kirk. In a Thursday court filing, the board argued that Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone erred in her recommendation, claiming "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence." The board's attorney contends that Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk, which labeled him as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi, was a "serious offense" warranting his removal.

Last month, Judge Livingstone issued an order recommending Theobald's reinstatement and awarded back pay and benefits, citing a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated First Amendment rights. According to an investigation report obtained by WPTV, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County deputies crack down on impaired driving ahead of July 4th weekend
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office is conducting enhanced patrols targeting impaired drivers during the Independence Day holiday period.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County deputies are conducting a crackdown on impaired driving as the July 4th weekend brings increased traffic to Treasure Coast roads. The enhanced enforcement effort targets drivers under the influence of alcohol or drugs during one of the busiest travel weekends of the year.

The Sheriff's Office announced the operation as part of holiday safety measures designed to reduce crashes and fatalities. Deputies are conducting increased patrols and checkpoints throughout St. Lucie County.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to receive 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: The City of Riviera Beach was named one of just 10 communities in the U.S. to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League and was the only Florida city selected.
cards.body:
Riviera Beach earned the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, becoming the only Florida city selected for the honor this year and one of just 10 U.S. communities to receive the award. The prestigious honor recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. The award was announced during the National Civic League conference in Denver, where Riviera Beach leaders presented the city's efforts to strengthen community engagement. Mayor Douglas Lawson called the recognition a proud moment for the city, stating that "Little old Riviera Beach is one of the biggest, brightest, shining stars." Lawson said the city earned the award through a long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents.

The city's application highlighted several civic engagement programs: the Riviera Beach Youth Council, which involves high school students in civic leadership and advocacy; the Citizens Leadership Academy with a 98% completion rate; and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program, which provides mini-grants to help longtime homeowners make critical repairs. City leaders say the recognition reflects years of work focused on improving civic health, strengthening trust between residents and local government, and creating opportunities for the community to play a direct role in shaping the city's future. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor, saying the award "brings back community pride." The All-America City Award has been presented annually since 1949.

hero.headline: Palm Beach County schools earn third straight A rating with record 93.5% graduation rate
hero.teaser: The School District of Palm Beach County received an A rating from the state for the third year in a row, with 84 percent of district-operated schools rated A or B.
hero.body:
The School District of Palm Beach County has received an A rating from the Florida Department of Education for the third consecutive year, reflecting strong student performance across all grade levels. The district reported that 143 of its operated schools, representing 84 percent of the total, earned either an A or B rating. This marks significant progress from the previous year, when 120 schools achieved these top two ratings. The state assigns grades to school districts and schools based on multiple factors, including student performance on state tests, graduation rates, and achievement in advanced coursework.

The district's success extends beyond school ratings to overall student achievement. The graduation rate reached a record-setting 93.5 percent, while 86 percent of seniors participated in college-level coursework by taking at least one Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education, or Dual Enrollment course. Additionally, 144 recent graduates earned an associate degree while still completing their high school diploma. Superintendent Mike Burke praised these accomplishments, stating that the A rating "reflects our ongoing commitment to sparking academic success and helping every student ignite their future."

One of the most dramatic success stories came from S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach, which jumped from a C rating to an A rating this year. The school had actually earned an A rating two years prior but narrowly missed a B rating last year. Principal Rona Tata, who has led the school for 15 years after five years as assistant principal, attributed the turnaround to a comprehensive approach. Three years ago, the school modified its early childhood curriculum program, which serves students starting at age 3 through kindergarten. Many of those students are now in third grade and performing at higher levels. Beyond curriculum changes, the school refined its entire academic approach, focusing on challenging both students and staff to raise expectations across campus. Tata said the school's theme last year was "Be the reason you succeed," which resonated with the school community.

Spady Elementary was one of four district schools that improved from a C rating to an A rating this year. The other three schools include Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary, and West Gate Elementary. Community members have expressed enthusiasm about Spady's transformation, noting that achieving an A rating will help attract students to their neighborhood school and demonstrate the district's commitment to educational excellence in the area.

cards.headline: Martin County Maritime Response Unit puts two boats on standby for Fourth of July boaters
cards.teaser: Martin County Maritime Response Unit will have two boats with medics on standby in the north and south county as hundreds of boaters hit the water this holiday weekend.
cards.body:
Lt. Brett Harry with Martin County Maritime Response Unit said hundreds of boaters are expected on the water this Fourth of July weekend. His team will have two boats with medics on standby positioned in both the north and south areas of Martin County to respond to anyone needing assistance. "We're just out there to mitigate anybody that needs help, whether it's something as simple as a stubbed toe to anything cardiac related, or potential spinal injuries, or anything like that," Harry said.

Boaters launched from the ramps Friday at Sandsprit Park in Martin County, including Brendan and Ashley Shannon with their young daughter and puppy. Harry emphasized that boaters should do their part to stay safe by keeping their eyes on the water, having a designated driver, and packing life vests, whistles and flotation devices. "Just have fun and be safe," Harry said.

cards.headline: Peacock House Art Foundation preserves Fort Pierce history and hosts artists from around the world
cards.teaser: The Peacock House Art Foundation in Fort Pierce operates in the historic Crain Estate and runs an artist-in-residency program attracting international artists.
cards.body:
The Peacock House Art Foundation is transforming Fort Pierce into an artistic destination by preserving the historic Crain Estate, the former home of Jaxson and Mary Crain. Mr. Crain was a tile worker whose craftsmanship is visible throughout the facility, from the ground to the walls to the ceiling. The couple traveled the world nine times, collecting one-of-a-kind items for their Florida estate, including a gazebo shipped from India. Visitors can take guided tours of the lush gardens and vibrant architecture every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. The foundation has made a conscious effort to preserve the estate's original character, keeping it approximately 90 percent the way it was when the Crains lived there.

The Peacock House gets its name from the birds that have roamed the property for decades. The Crains are believed to have introduced peacocks to Fort Pierce in the 1970s, originally bringing in seven birds that have since grown to over 100. Among the flock is Bob, believed to be 60 years old and the oldest peacock on the property, recognizable by his limp. Bob is hand-fed daily and has his own bowls. The foundation's artist-in-residency program attracts artists from around the world and offers simple but elegant accommodations. The art lab provides classes for children and adults of all skill levels, with instructors like Krystal Masters leading one-on-one classes designed for complete beginners.

cards.headline: Breast cancer patient's insurance denies reconstruction surgery hours before procedure
cards.teaser: Beth Clark, 48, had her breast reconstruction surgery denied by Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield less than 24 hours before the scheduled procedure.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed three months ago with invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common type of breast cancer. She underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction planned using GalaFlex, a synthetic surgical mesh. Less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure. According to her denial letter, the surgery is still considered investigational and there is no or not enough proof it improves health.

GalaFlex is popular among plastic surgeons and approved by the FDA for some uses in the body, but it is not approved for breast reconstruction and is still considered an off-label, investigational, and experimental treatment. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated its "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined." Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and says the product gives her patients the least amount of complications. Despite the insurer's denial, Clark got her reconstruction surgery with the GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week ago. A spokesperson with Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield said the company regularly reviews coverage policies and that the GalaFlex mesh is not FDA-approved for breast reconstruction surgery and does not currently meet the standards required for coverage by its medical policy.

hero.headline: Martin County School Board fights judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk Facebook comments
hero.teaser: The Martin County School Board is pushing back against a judge's recommendation to reinstate a teacher suspended last year following controversial social media .
hero.body:
The Martin County School Board is pushing back against a judge's recommendation to reinstate a teacher suspended last year following controversial social media comments about Charlie Kirk. Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009, sparked controversy with his comments, which labeled Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi. In a Thursday court filing, the school board argued Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone erred in recommending Theobald get his job back, saying "numerous findings ... are not based upon competent substantial evidence." The board's attorney claims Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk was a "serious offense" and removing him was appropriate.

In an order issued last month, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated the teacher's First Amendment rights. The judge also recommended Theobald be awarded back pay and benefits. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments about Kirk but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page "within a discussion among personal acquaintances" and were not intended for public view. The school board still has the final say on whether Theobald gets his job back. After the judge's recommendation, Theobald told WPTV the case raises a larger question about where the line is drawn for teachers speaking outside of school.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie council moves forward on land transfer for Midway Road Florida Turnpike interchange
cards.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation for a partial interchange at Midway Road and the Florida Turnpike.
cards.body:
Last month, the Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of an ordinance to give 7 acres of land to the Florida Department of Transportation to assist with the interchange. Scott Samples, strategic communications manager for Port St. Lucie, said there is a significant gap between the entrances and exits to the Turnpike currently in Port St. Lucie. The interchange is designed to accommodate the growth that has already occurred and the growth that will occur over the next 20 to 50 years.

FDOT has been constructing the $95 million Midway Road Widening Project to help with congestion and safety. Crews are currently working on the first phase, widening the road from two lanes to four lanes from Selvitz Road to Jenkins Road. According to the FDOT website for the project, the second widening phase from Jenkins Road to Glades Cut Off Road is still in the design phase and construction is anticipated to begin in Summer 2027.

FDOT is also working on improving the Turnpike bridge and adding a partial interchange for the Turnpike. The partial interchange is still in the design phase. Erin Scheumeister, a Port St. Lucie resident, said the construction can be annoying but she believes it is necessary and will make it easier to get to work. City council will vote on final approval to give the land at an upcoming meeting.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce breast cancer patient denied insurance coverage hours before reconstruction surgery
cards.teaser: Beth Clark's insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for a reconstruction procedure less than 24 hours before it was scheduled, citing the surgical mesh as investigational.
cards.body:
Beth Clark, 48, was diagnosed three months ago with invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common type of breast cancer. She underwent a full double bilateral mastectomy with reconstruction, but less than 24 hours before her reconstruction surgery, her insurance company, Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield, denied coverage for the procedure. According to her denial letter, the surgery involving a surgical mesh called GalaFlex is still considered "investigational" and "there is no or not enough proof it improves health." GalaFlex is a synthetic surgical mesh approved by the FDA for some uses in the body but not for breast reconstruction. In a 2023 letter to health care providers, the FDA stated its "efficacy and safety for breast cancer patients have not been determined."

Dr. Alicia Billington, Clark's plastic surgeon, uses GalaFlex mesh on most of her breast reconstruction patients and says the product gives her patients the least amount of complications. Billington has been a vocal critic of insurance denials and recently shared Clark's denial on social media calling for policy changes. An Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield spokesperson said the company regularly reviews coverage policies to ensure they are based on medical evidence and aligned with the latest treatment standards, but noted the mesh does not currently meet the standards required for coverage by their medical policy. Despite the denial, Clark received her reconstruction surgery with the GalaFlex mesh a little more than a week ago. Last year, Cigna became the first and only major insurer to start approving GalaFlex for breast reconstruction.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County marine deputies rescue 2 boaters after vessel sinks in Intracoastal Waterway
cards.teaser: Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on Wednesday. Both occupants ended up in the water but were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived.
cards.body:
Two boaters are safe after their vessel sank in the Intracoastal Waterway on July 1, thanks to a quick response from the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Marine Unit and a life-saving decision to wear life jackets. The Marine Unit responded to reports of a small motorized boat taking on water and becoming submerged. Body-worn camera footage captured the rescue as it unfolded. Both occupants ended up in the water when their boat went down, but deputies say they were wearing life jackets that kept them afloat while help arrived.

Marine Unit deputies quickly located the pair in the water and safely brought them aboard their patrol vessel. The boaters were then transported back to the boat ramp without any injuries reported. "This incident serves as an important reminder that wearing a life jacket can save your life," the sheriff's office said in a Facebook post. "We're grateful this call ended safely and proud of the swift response by our Marine Unit deputies who are always ready to answer the call."

cards.headline: Hobe Sound community raises funds for man who lost fiancée Misty Dawn White in deadly home fire
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside the couple's home. Friends have launched a fundraiser to help her fiancé Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings.
cards.body:
A Hobe Sound man is receiving community support after losing his fiancée, Misty Dawn White, 46, in a deadly home fire earlier this week. White was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside the couple's home. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause, though the fire remains under investigation. Friends have since launched a fundraiser to help Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings.

Nina Fenn, a friend of White's for eight years, spoke about the loss and reflected on how White should be remembered. "Misty was a Christian woman. She loved gardening and plants. She plays the piano," Fenn said, adding that White "was always the first to lend a hand" and loved children and people. The timing of White's death compounds the tragedy, as Misty's birthday is the Fourth of July and she passed just days before it. Fenn also noted that Mark has endured previous tragedy, having lost his only child, Jacob. "She'll always be in our hearts," Fenn said of White.

cards.headline: Peacock House Art Foundation in Fort Pierce offers art classes and tours of historic Crain Estate
cards.teaser: The Peacock House Art Foundation is transforming Fort Pierce into an artistic destination, preserving the legacy of Jaxson and Mary Crain and connecting local and international artists through its artist-in-residency program.
cards.body:
Rewritten Card Body:

Tucked away in the historic Crain Estate, the Peacock House Art Foundation preserves the legacy of Jaxson and Mary Crain, who once called the property home. Mr. Crain was a tile worker by trade, and his craftsmanship is visible throughout the facility, from the ground to the walls to the ceiling. Many parts of the house remain largely unchanged from when the Crains lived there, including the smoking and bourbon room with its man paneling and ornate stained glass that leads out to a bar on the front patio. The couple traveled the world nine times, collecting one-of-a-kind items including a gazebo shipped from India. Visitors can take guided tours of the lush gardens and vibrant architecture every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

The foundation gets its name from the peacocks that have roamed the property for decades. The Crains are believed to have introduced the birds to Fort Pierce in the 1970s, originally bringing in seven peacocks that have since grown to over 100. Among the flock is Bob, believed to be the oldest peacock on the property at 60 years old, known for walking with a limp and receiving daily hand-feedings. The foundation's artist-in-residency program attracts artists from around the world. Art director Krystal Masters leads one-on-one classes in the art lab designed for complete beginners, offering mediums including sculpting and watercolor. Masters describes art as a form of therapy that helps people leave happy.

cards.headline: Stuart's downtown dock closes Monday for $3 million renovation to nearly double slip capacity
cards.body:
Stuart's downtown public dock will close July 6 for a $3 million renovation expected to be complete by next Fourth of July. The project will nearly double the dock's capacity, expanding from 18 to 44 slips for both motorized and non-motorized vessels. Funded by a state grant and transportation impact fees, the renovation will add a 7,500 square foot fixed dock, a 1,400 square foot floating dock, and a smaller floating platform. Stuart Mayor Sean Reed said the upgrades serve a critical purpose beyond increasing capacity. "They're doing it to prevent storm damage during hurricanes and major storms," Reed said. "So the year of waiting will be worth it." The dock currently serves more than 1,400 boaters annually.

During the closure, the city is accommodating businesses that depend on the dock. Tiki Taxi & Cruises, which operates from the dock, initially worried about continuing operations during construction. The city found a solution by allowing the company to build a gate at the end of the downtown Stuart dock on the non-floating section. Austin Kuyrkendall, director of operations for Tiki Taxi & Cruises, supports the expansion. "Stuart is not Stuart without the water," Kuyrkendall said. He noted the dock's current constraints, particularly on weekends. "On the weekend that's when it can get a little hectic at the dock and you know it's never great for us when we're squeezing in and trying to find spots," Kuyrkendall said.

hero.body:

The project will nearly double the dock's capacity, expanding from 18 to 44 slips for motorized and non-motorized vessels. The renovation includes a 7,500 square foot fixed dock, a 1,400 square foot floating dock and a smaller floating platform. The project is funded by a state grant and transportation impact fees.

Stuart Mayor Sean Reed said the upgrades are designed to prevent storm damage during hurricanes and major storms. More than 1,400 boaters use the dock annually. During the closure, the city is working to accommodate businesses relying on the dock. Tiki Taxi & Cruises, which operates from the dock, will be allowed to build a gate at the end of the non-floating section to continue boarding passengers, according to Austin Kuyrkendall, the company's director of operations. Boat captain Parker Fisher said the dock has needed work for years and hopes to see more floating docks added to the facility.

cards.headline: Martin County School Board challenges judge's order to reinstate teacher suspended over Charlie Kirk post
cards.teaser: The Martin County School Board filed a court document Thursday fighting a judge's recommendation to reinstate Matt Theobald, a Spectrum Academy teacher suspended for Facebook comments about Charlie Kirk.
cards.body:
Matt Theobald, a social studies teacher at Spectrum Academy since 2009, was suspended last year after making social media comments labeling Charlie Kirk as racist, misogynistic and a neo-Nazi. Administrative Law Judge Jodi-Ann Vanessa Livingstone recommended last month that Theobald be reinstated with back pay and benefits. In her order, Livingstone cited a recent Florida Fifth District Court of Appeal ruling that said disciplining a teacher for personal Facebook posts made off school grounds, on personal equipment, with no student involvement, violated First Amendment rights.

In a Thursday court filing, the Martin County School Board argued that numerous findings in Livingstone's order are not based on competent substantial evidence. The board's attorney called Theobald's Facebook post about Kirk a "serious offense" and said removing him was appropriate. According to an investigation report, Theobald admitted writing the comments but said they were posted on his mother's private Facebook page within a discussion among personal acquaintances and were not intended for public view. The school board retains final authority on whether Theobald returns to his position, with no timeline set for a decision.

cards.headline: Hobe Sound woman dies in house fire, community raises funds for fiance
cards.teaser: Misty Dawn White, 46, died Monday in a Hobe Sound house fire that preliminary findings suggest was caused by an electrical issue. Friends have launched a fundraiser for her fiance Mark.
cards.body:
Misty Dawn White, 46, was found dead Monday after a fire broke out inside her Hobe Sound home. Preliminary findings from the sheriff's office point to an electrical issue as a possible cause. The fire remains under investigation. Friends have since launched a fundraiser to help White's fiancé Mark rebuild after the flames destroyed many of his and White's belongings.

Nina Fenn, a friend of White's for eight years, learned of the death through a phone call from Mark. "It's completely a state of devastation," Fenn said. Fenn described White as a Christian woman who loved gardening, plants, playing piano, kids and people, and was always the first to lend a hand. The loss is compounded by grief Mark has already endured after losing his only child, Jacob. White's birthday is July 4, just days after her death on Monday.

cards.headline: Riviera Beach named only Florida city to receive 2026 All-America City Award
cards.teaser: Riviera Beach was selected as one of just 10 communities nationwide to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, the only Florida city honored this year.
cards.body:
Riviera Beach was named one of 10 communities in the United States to receive the 2026 All-America City Award from the National Civic League, becoming the only Florida city selected for the honor. The award recognizes communities that bring residents, local government, businesses and organizations together to solve local challenges and create lasting change. City leaders presented Riviera Beach's efforts to strengthen community engagement at the National Civic League conference in Denver, where judges announced the city as a first-time winner. Mayor Douglas Lawson said the city earned the award through a long-term effort to revitalize Riviera Beach and improve quality of life for residents. "They're seeing the changes; they're seeing the revitalization and the reimagining of Riviera Beach that we set out so many years to do," Lawson said.

Riviera Beach's application highlighted several civic engagement programs including the Riviera Beach Youth Council for high school students, the Citizens Leadership Academy with a 98 percent completion rate, and the Neighborhood Reclaim Home Rehabilitation Program providing mini-grants to longtime homeowners. Councilwoman KaShamba Miller-Anderson credited residents for the honor, stating "Every event we host, every project we complete, and every challenge we overcome happens because our community shows up for one another." She said winning the award reinforces the city's positive momentum and positions the community for future opportunities and continued growth.

Head coach Jimmy Robertson noted that most of the seniors are four-year players who came through the program's middle school system, providing continuity and experience. The Scots have scheduled more challenging opponents for the fall to prepare for deeper playoff runs. Senior Jack Williams said the demanding schedule reflects the program's desire to compete at the next level and attract new players. The team's primary postseason goal is advancing beyond the second round of playoffs. Senior Jack Whelche emphasized that going undefeated in the regular season does not matter if the team continues losing in the second round. The players are using summer workouts as motivation for the upcoming season. Senior Edmyer St. Jean said the daily training sessions provide something to work toward as the team prepares to potentially break their program record.

hero.headline: Loggerhead Marinelife Center in Juno Beach offers sea turtle nesting programs through September

Guests can participate in guided Turtle Walks, the Hatchling Discovery Program, Hatchling Releases, Tidal Tots and Plastic Free July Community Action Day. The Turtle Walk program allows participants to observe the nesting process while learning about sea turtle biology, conservation and ongoing research efforts. Educational demonstrations may include the use of red-light headlamps, amber lighting, night scopes and research tag scanning equipment.

The center's education and research departments work together during nesting season to collect and analyze data related to nesting activity and hatchling success. Sea turtle nesting season in Florida typically runs from March through October. Conservation groups encourage beachgoers to turn off beachfront lighting at night, properly dispose of trash and avoid disturbing nesting turtles or hatchlings. Registration information and program details are available through Loggerhead Marinelife Center.

hero.body:
Rewritten Card Body

The Florida Department of Environmental Protection announced free admission to state parks from Friday, July 3, 2026, through Sunday, July 5, 2026, to celebrate America's 250th anniversary. DEP Secretary Alexis A. invited all Floridians, their friends, and family to explore the outdoors and make new memories at the state's public lands. The initiative applies to day use only at most parks, with overnight accommodations, special events, concessions, and rentals still requiring payment.

Florida's state park system is the only four-time winner of the NRPA's National Gold Medal Award. The parks offer hiking, camping, wildlife viewing, swimming, paddling, horseback riding, and access to historic sites including forts, battlefields, and archaeological landmarks. Over the last fiscal year, Florida State Parks recorded more than 28 million visitors, generating an estimated $3.6 billion in statewide economic impact. Three locations are excluded from the free admission weekend: Ellie Schiller Homosassa Springs Wildlife State Park, Skyway Fishing Pier State Park, and Weeki Wachee Springs State Park. Visitors can plan trips at FloridaStateParks.org.

cards.headline: DeSantis signs $117.6 billion Florida budget with $810 million in vetoes
cards.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a $117.6 billion state budget this week, marking the fourth consecutive year of declining spending in Florida. The Governor vetoed nearly $810 million in line-item projects, exercising restraint compared to his record-breaking $3.1 billion in vetoes in 2022. DeSantis said he cut items considered either inappropriate or nice to have, focusing the budget on what he characterized as core state priorities.

The approved budget invests billions in road construction acceleration, teacher pay increases, and major cancer research initiatives. The spending plan sets aside $665 million for Everglades restoration efforts. However, DeSantis also blocked the Legislature's proposed $750 million transfer into the state's rainy-day fund, which lawmakers included to prepare for new requirements under a proposed constitutional amendment passed by the House last year that would increase the mandated cap on the budget stabilization fund.

Among the notable cuts, DeSantis vetoed $91.5 million intended to increase correctional officers' salaries. Government watchdog Florida TaxWatch had urged the Governor to eliminate 621 projects worth $830 million that the group labeled budget turkeys. DeSantis ultimately vetoed 184 of the 621 appropriations flagged by the organization.

The term-limited Governor indicated he will not formally lead any political committee to campaign for budget-related constitutional amendments after the Legislature modified his original proposals. DeSantis said that while he might participate if asked, he does not plan to spearhead efforts or take a leadership role in advocating for the changes. The new fiscal year budget took effect as DeSantis approaches the end of his final term as Florida's chief executive.

cards.headline: Southwest Florida communities stage fireworks, parades and drone shows for semiquincentennial
cards.teaser: Communities across Southwest Florida are marking America's 250th birthday with celebrations from Sarasota's bayfront to Fort Myers Beach.
cards.body:
Fourth of July weekend brought fireworks, parades, drone shows and waterfront celebrations across Southwest Florida as communities marked America's 250th birthday. Festivities spanned from Sarasota's bayfront and Nathan Benderson Park to Manatee County, Venice, North Port and Fort Myers Beach. Anna Maria Island hosted the Privateers' annual water parade beginning in the Coquina Beach and Bradenton Beach area, while Bradenton and Palmetto celebrated jointly along the Manatee River with activities at the Bradenton Riverwalk, Rossi Park, Old Main Street and Palmetto's Riverside Park, which featured Palmetto's 15th annual Fourth Fest with 14 food trucks and 20 artisan vendors.

Sarasota's bayfront hosted the America250 fireworks display at 9 p.m., while Waterside Place in Lakewood Ranch at 1560 Lakefront Drive featured circus acts, carnival games and a drone show at 9 p.m. Siesta Beach held its 35th annual community fireworks show, 100% funded by local residents, businesses and community supporters, running from 8 to 9:30 p.m. Venice celebrated with a patriotic parade through Historic Downtown beginning at 9:30 a.m. at West Venice Avenue and Avenue des Parques, plus an evening fireworks show at the South Jetty starting between 9 to 9:15 p.m., with contingency plans to reschedule to July 5. North Port's Freedom Festival: Cheers to 250 Years at CoolToday Park ran from 6 to 9:30 p.m. with fireworks at 9 p.m., while Fort Myers Beach kicked off with a parade at 10 a.m. from Bay Oaks Recreation Center down Estero Boulevard to Times Square, followed by fireworks around 9 p.m. from a barge near Times Square.

cards.headline: Marion County stages four synchronized fireworks displays for America's 250th
cards.teaser: Ocala and Marion County are celebrating the semiquincentennial with synchronized fireworks at four locations and a parade through the city.
cards.body:
Marion County staged four synchronized fireworks displays on July 4 to commemorate America's 250th anniversary under the Marion Celebrates 250 banner. Each location began at 5 p.m. with live entertainment, food vendors, and family activities before fireworks at 9 p.m. The sites included Veterans Memorial Park in Ocala, Wrigley Fields in Citra, Dunnellon High School in Dunnellon, and the Belleview Sportsplex in Belleview. The celebration marked the semiquincentennial, the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, as part of America250, the nonpartisan initiative of the U.S. Semiquincentennial Commission.

The city of Ocala hosted Fourth in the Park at Tuscawilla Park starting at 10 a.m., featuring live music, food trucks, a kids zone, and games. Country singer-songwriter Emma Forgette performed from 10 to 11:30 a.m., followed by Nashville recording artist Cliff Dorsey from noon to 2 p.m. The city also opened its aquatic fun centers, splash pads, and the Discovery Center for free. The Patriot Parade kicked off at Southeast 16th Avenue, proceeded to Silver Springs Boulevard, and turned to finish near Southeast 25th Avenue, featuring veteran groups, local businesses, and community organizations. Marion County promoted its Explore Your Freedom Here theme throughout the summer, highlighting crystal-clear springs, hiking trails, the World Equestrian Center, and locally owned restaurants and breweries.

hero.headline: Record Fourth of July travel brings heavy traffic and rain to South Florida roads
hero.body:
A record-breaking number of Americans are hitting the roads this Fourth of July weekend, and South Florida drivers are contending with both massive crowds and heavy rain. AAA estimates that 72.2 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles from home between Saturday, June 27 and Sunday, July 5, marking an all-time high for the holiday. Of those travelers, 61.4 million are making the journey by car. Orlando and Miami rank among the top five travel destinations for Independence Day this year, according to AAA data. Friday's wet weather created challenging conditions on the Florida Turnpike south of Orlando as drivers began their holiday trips.

The combination of rain and congestion tested drivers' abilities on the roadways. Driver Ed Budd described the conditions as beautiful until the rain arrived, at which point he observed that everyone seemed to forget how to drive. Despite the challenging weather, most drivers pressed forward with their plans. Driver Jim Macfawn, who said he has considerable driving experience, explained that he simply rolls with the punches when dealing with difficult road conditions. Macfawn also reflected on the scale of holiday travel, expressing surprise at the number of people traveling given current gas prices.

Some drivers experienced very different outcomes on Friday's roads. Carlos Borras and his wife completed a round trip between Orlando and Miami without incident, reporting smooth sailing with no traffic or accidents encountered. Driver Fernando Amado painted a different picture, describing busy conditions that were made worse by the weather. Amado noted that Friday appeared to be the peak day for people heading north, contrary to what some might have expected.

For those still planning to travel, AAA offers guidance on timing. The organization recommends leaving after 3 p.m. on Saturday or before 11 a.m. on Sunday to avoid the worst congestion. Saturday's heaviest traffic is expected between 10 a.m., while Sunday will see peak congestion between noon and 6 p.m. According to AAA, your starting point, destination, and departure time all play significant roles in determining your travel experience. With record numbers of vehicles on South Florida roads this weekend, careful planning about when to travel can make a substantial difference in avoiding delays.

hero.headline: AAA estimates 72.2 million Americans traveling this Fourth of July weekend, South Florida roads jammed
hero.teaser: Record Fourth of July travel brought heavy traffic and rain to South Florida roads Friday, with the Florida Turnpike south of Orlando experiencing wet conditions and crowded highways.
hero.body:
A record-breaking number of Americans are hitting the road this Independence Day weekend, with AAA estimating that 72.2 million people will travel at least 50 miles from home between Saturday, June 27 and Sunday, July 5. This marks an all-time high for Fourth of July travel. Of those travelers, 61.4 million are choosing to drive rather than fly or use other transportation methods. Orlando and Miami have both ranked among the top five travel destinations for this holiday period, making South Florida roads particularly congested during this busy weekend.

Wet weather on Friday added another layer of difficulty to the already crowded Florida Turnpike, especially for drivers heading south from Orlando. Several drivers described their experiences navigating the challenging conditions. "Really beautiful until it starts raining and then everyone forgets how to drive," said driver Ed Budd, referencing the impact that bad weather has on driving behavior during peak travel times. Despite the obstacles, many travelers continued their journeys undeterred. Jim Macfawn noted his approach to handling the situation: "I have a lot of experience driving, so I just roll with the punches." However, not all drivers experienced heavy traffic. Carlos Borras and his wife completed their round trip between Orlando and Miami on Friday without incident, reporting smooth conditions. "I don't think I saw any traffic, no accidents or anything, so it's been great," Borras said.

The sheer volume of travelers this year caught some drivers by surprise. Macfawn reflected on the scale of the holiday travel numbers, saying: "It sounds like a lot. I'm surprised people can afford all the gas." Meanwhile, Fernando Amado reported a busier experience, noting: "It's been pretty busy, especially with the weather. I thought people were leaving yesterday, but today is the day when people are really heading up North." These varied experiences highlight how timing, location, and weather conditions can dramatically affect travel experiences during peak holiday periods.

For those still planning to travel over the weekend, AAA offers specific recommendations to help drivers avoid the worst traffic congestion. The organization advises travelers to leave after 3 p.m. on Saturday or before 11 a.m. on Sunday for the smoothest driving conditions. The heaviest congestion is expected to occur between 10 a.m. on Saturday and between noon and 6 p.m. on Sunday. By planning departure times strategically and staying informed about traffic patterns, drivers can improve their chances of reaching their destinations safely and efficiently.

cards.headline: Peacock House Art Foundation transforms Fort Pierce historic estate into arts destination with global artist residencies
cards.teaser: The Peacock House Art Foundation is transforming Fort Pierce into an artistic destination through a historic estate that now serves as the centerpiece of the Pe.
cards.body:
The Peacock House Art Foundation is transforming Fort Pierce into an artistic destination through the historic Crain Estate, the former home of Jaxson and Mary Crain. Jaxson Crain was a tile worker whose craftsmanship is visible throughout the facility, from ground to walls to ceiling. The couple traveled the world nine times and collected one-of-a-kind items for their Florida property, including a gazebo shipped from India. Guided tours of the gardens and architecture are available every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. The estate remains 90 percent the way it was when the Crains lived there, including a smoking and bourbon room with man paneling and stained glass. The foundation has made a conscious effort to preserve the estate's original character without commercializing it.

The Crains are believed to have introduced peacocks to Fort Pierce in the 1970s, bringing in seven birds that have multiplied to over 100 on the property. One peacock named Bob is believed to be 60 years old and walks with a limp. According to art director Krystal Masters, Bob is a spoiled peacock with his own bowls and gets hand-fed every day. The foundation runs an artist-in-residency program that attracts artists from around the world, providing simple but elegant accommodations. The art lab offers classes for children and adults of all skill levels, including one-on-one instruction where students with zero experience walk out with a finished piece of art.

The survey points to inflation as the driver behind increased costs. Ground beef is up 5.5%, and buns are up 7.7%. Strawberries, hit hard by a Florida frost, are up 12.4%. Ice cream is up 5.3%.

Not all items are more expensive this year. Potato prices are down, offering savings for potato chip and salad lovers. Corn prices have fluctuated, but locally grown corn from the Glades can offer the best deal. Budgeting expert Andrea Woroch recommends families compare stores to find the best deals on their grocery lists and cut down on food waste by creating a meal plan.

cards.headline: Palm Beach County schools earn third consecutive A rating from state
cards.teaser: The School District of Palm Beach County received an A rating from the state for the third year in a row, with 143 district-operated schools rated A or B.
cards.body:
The School District of Palm Beach County earned an A rating from the Florida Department of Education for the third consecutive year, reflecting strong student performance across all grade levels. This year, 143 district-operated schools, or 84 percent, received A or B ratings, an increase from 120 schools the previous year. The district achieved a record-setting 93.5 percent graduation rate, and 86 percent of seniors participated in college-level coursework, including Advanced Placement, International Baccalaureate, Cambridge Advanced International Certificate of Education, or Dual Enrollment courses. Additionally, 144 recent graduates earned an associate degree alongside their high school diploma.

S.D. Spady Elementary School in Delray Beach achieved the year's most dramatic turnaround, jumping from a C rating to an A rating. Principal Rona Tata, who has served in the role for 15 years, attributed the improvement to curriculum modifications made three years ago in the school's early childhood program, which serves students starting at age 3 through kindergarten. Three other district schools also improved from C to A ratings: Dwight D. Eisenhower K-8, Glade View Elementary, and West Gate Elementary. According to Tata, the school had previously earned an A rating two years ago and narrowly missed a B rating last year by just a few points.
